Precipitating factors: GI bleed, infection (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, TB, malaria), electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, alkalosis), constipation, excess dietary protein, sedatives (benzodiazepines, opioids), renal dysfunction
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP): High prevalence of ascites and limited early presentation

qs.q: Which class of intravenous antibiotics is a common choice for empirical coverage when spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is suspected in a child with nephrotic syndrome?
qs.e: A third-generation cephalosporin is a common choice of intravenous antibiotic because it provides broad enough coverage to include Pneumococcus and Gram-negative bacteria. Blood and peritoneal cultures should be drawn first.

qs.q: What is the defining ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count threshold used to diagnose Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
o: Ascitic absolute neutrophil count less than 50 cells/ul
Ascitic absolute neutrophil count greater than 500 cells/ul
Ascitic absolute neutrophil count greater than 250 cells/ul
Ascitic absolute neutrophil count exactly 100 cells/ul
qs.e: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is defined by an ascitic neutrophil count greater than 250 cells/ul with a pure growth of a single organism and no surgically correctable cause. A lower count would generally rule out this diagnosis.

qs.q: Which of the following organisms is noted as one of the most common causative agents of Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis?
qs.e: E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and pneumococcus are listed as the most common agents responsible for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Anaerobes account for only about 1% of cases.

qs.q: When managing a patient with Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis, what is the recommended action if the ascitic fluid PMN count has not decreased by at least 25% after 2 days of treatment?
o: Perform an urgent liver transplantation procedure
Double the daily dose of oral spironolactone
qs.e: The text states that clinicians should re-evaluate if the ascitic fluid PMN count has not decreased by at least 25% after 2 days of treatment. Stopping antibiotics prematurely without re-evaluation would be clinically inappropriate.

qs.q: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites develops peritonitis. Which bacterium is a common cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in this population?
qs.e: While *E. coli* is the most common cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), *S. pneumoniae* is also a recognized cause, particularly in patients with cirrhosis and ascites. *S. aureus* and *P. aeruginosa* are less commonly associated with SBP.

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with known cirrhosis is admitted with diffuse abdominal tenderness and a low-grade fever. Diagnostic paracentesis is performed to rule out spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Which laboratory finding confirms this diagnosis?
o: Ascitic fluid total protein concentration over 3.0 g/dL
Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear count above 250 cells/uL
Ascitic fluid lactate dehydrogenase level exceeding 400 U/L
Positive ascitic fluid fungal culture on Sabouraud agar
qs.e: An ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear leukocyte count greater than 250 cells/uL establishes the diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis regardless of culture results. Total protein levels are variable and do not serve as the primary diagnostic threshold.

qs.q: A cirrhotic patient develops spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and requires antimicrobial therapy. Which antibiotic class serves as the standard initial treatment covering the majority of causative flora?
qs.e: Third-generation cephalosporins like cefotaxime cover approximately 95% of the flora responsible for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. First-generation agents lack adequate Gram-negative coverage for this indication.

qs.q: What peritoneal fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) cell count threshold indicates spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?
qs.e: A PMN count greater than 250/mm3 in the ascitic fluid analysis indicates spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Elevated WBC counts can also signal general inflammation or infection.

es.q: Discuss the clinical features, diagnosis, and management principles of Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP).
es.m:
- **Definition:** Ascitic fluid infection with a pure growth of a single organism and an ascitic neutrophil count greater than 250 cells/mcL without a surgically correctable cause.
- **Common causative agents:** Includes E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and pneumococcus.
- **Clinical presentation:** Present in 85% of patients with fever, abdominal pain, and a change in mental status.
- **Empirical treatment:** Treated with 3rd generation cephalosporins (such as IV cefotaxime), amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, or oral norfloxacin for uncomplicated cases.
- **Treatment exclusions and monitoring:** Aminoglycosides are avoided; re-evaluation is required if the PMN count does not drop by at least 25%

ai.title: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: SBP is an infection of ascitic fluid without an intra‑abdominal source, most common in cirrhosis. Diagnosis relies on ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ and clinical suspicion. Prompt antibiotics and albumin improve survival.

sections.p: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs when bacteria translocate from the gut lumen into ascitic fluid, usually in patients with decompensated cirrhosis. It presents with fever, abdominal pain or tenderness, and worsening encephalopathy, but may be subtle in low‑resource settings.
b: Most common in cirrhosis with ascites
Precipitating factors: GI bleed, recent antibiotics, HIV, TB, malaria

sections.p: Gram‑negative enteric bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella) cause ~70 % of cases; gram‑positive cocci (Streptococcus, Enterococcus) account for the rest. Anaerobes are rare but reported in some African series.
b: Enteric bacteria dominate because of increased gut permeability
Antibiotic resistance patterns may reflect local HIV/TB drug use

sections.p: No external transmission; bacteria cross the intestinal mucosa (bacterial translocation) facilitated by portal hypertension, low protein in ascitic fluid, and immune dysfunction.
b: Portal hypertension → intestinal edema → bacterial overgrowth
Low ascitic complement and opsonins impair clearance

sections.p: Infection of sterile ascitic fluid leads to peritoneal inflammation, systemic sepsis, renal dysfunction (hepatorenal syndrome), and can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
b: Acute kidney injury is the leading cause of early death
Progressive encephalopathy may mask abdominal signs

sections.p: Diagnosis rests on paracentesis with cell count and culture. In low‑resource hospitals, bedside microscopy and rapid Gram stain guide early therapy when culture facilities are absent.

t.b: Is SBP present? – ≥250 cells/mm³ confirms infection
What organism is likely? – Presence of Gram‑negative rods suggests enteric bacteria; guides empiric choice
Is ascites portal‑hypertensive? – SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL supports cirrhotic ascites, the typical setting for SBP
Is renal dysfunction developing? – Rising creatinine signals hepatorenal syndrome, prompting albumin

sections.p: Start empiric third‑generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefotaxime) immediately after paracentesis, plus intravenous albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 to prevent renal failure. Adjust antibiotics when culture results return.
b: Cefotaxime chosen for broad Gram‑negative coverage and low nephrotoxicity
Avoid aminoglycosides in cirrhosis because of renal risk
If cephalosporin unavailable, use ampicillin‑sulbactam if local resistance is low

sections.p: Key bedside steps: (1) suspect SBP in any cirrhotic patient with new fever, pain or encephalopathy; (2) perform urgent paracentesis; (3) start antibiotics before results; (4) give albumin if creatinine rises or baseline >1 mg/dL; (5) monitor for renal failure and encephalopathy.
b: Paracentesis is safe even in coagulopathy; delay increases mortality
A neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ is diagnostic regardless of culture
Prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., norfloxacin) after an episode reduce recurrence

whenToSeekHelp: Septic shock (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status)

faq.a: Rarely; it can be seen in nephrotic syndrome or peritoneal dialysis, but cirrhosis accounts for >90 % of cases.

faq.q: Why is albumin given with antibiotics?
faq.a: Albumin expands intravascular volume, improves renal perfusion, and reduces the risk of hepatorenal syndrome.

faq.q: What if the ascitic fluid culture is negative?
faq.a: A neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³ still confirms SBP; treat empirically.

exam: A cirrhotic patient presents with fever and mild abdominal tenderness – what is your immediate next step? — Perform diagnostic paracentesis before any imaging.
Ascitic fluid shows 300 cells/mm³ neutrophils, Gram stain negative – how do you interpret this? — Meets SBP criteria; start empiric antibiotics despite negative stain.
Why is cefotaxime preferred over ciprofloxacin for initial SBP therapy? — Better Gram‑negative coverage, lower resistance, and safer in renal impairment.
A patient on prophylactic norfloxacin develops SBP – what does this indicate about the organism? — Likely resistant gram‑positive or atypical organism; modify antibiotics based on culture.
How does bacterial translocation lead to SBP in portal hypertension? — Increased intestinal permeability, bacterial overgrowth, and impaired immune clearance allow organisms to enter ascitic fluid.
What are the indications for giving albumin in SBP? — Serum creatinine >1 mg/dL or BUN >30 mg/dL, or development of hepatorenal syndrome.

Differentiate SBP from tuberculous peritonitis in a low‑resource setting. — SBP: acute fever, neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³, rapid response to antibiotics; TB: subacute, lymphocyte‑predominant ascites, low neutrophils, poor response to cephalosporins.
What are the key warning signs that require urgent transfer to a higher‑level facility? — Septic shock, rapidly rising creatinine, refractory encephalopathy, massive hemorrhage.
